subject.name: First Language English
subject.description: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English. Topics follow the questions of Paper 1 (Reading) and Paper 2 (Directed Writing and Composition), so you can practise each part of each paper. All passages and questions are original practice material written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material. Writing tasks are self-marked against a criteria checklist modelled on the Cambridge mark scheme split between content, structure, style and accuracy.

topics.title: Question 1: comprehension
topics.summary: Short-answer questions on Text A: finding explicit information and explaining what is implied.

topics.title: Question 1(f): summary
topics.summary: Selecting relevant points from Text B and writing a concise summary in your own words.

topics.title: Question 2(a)–(c): vocabulary and explaining meaning
topics.summary: Explaining the meaning of words and phrases in your own words, and the effect of a single image.

topics.title: Question 2(d): language analysis
topics.summary: Selecting powerful words and images and explaining how the writer uses them to create effects.

topics.title: Question 3: extended response to reading
topics.summary: Writing as a character (a letter, journal, interview or speech) using and developing ideas from the text.

topics.title: Question 1: directed writing
topics.summary: Evaluating ideas from one or two texts in a letter, article or speech for a given audience.

topics.title: Composition: descriptive writing
topics.summary: Creating atmosphere and detail with precise vocabulary and varied sentences.

topics.title: Composition: narrative writing
topics.summary: Writing a well-structured story with convincing characters and setting.

questions.stem:
Passage A: The Crossing

I had been awake since four, listening to the generator next door cough itself into life. My school bag sat by the door, packed and repacked twice. When my mother handed me a cup of tea, my hands would not keep it still, and I left half of it cooling on the step.

The boat left the jetty at 5:40, exactly as Mr Okafor had promised. There were six of us on board: four children in pressed white shirts, a woman with a basket of mangoes, and me. Nobody spoke. At that hour the water was a sheet of hammered pewter, and the far shore was nothing more than a rumour of trees.

Halfway across, the engine faltered. It did not stop; it hesitated, like a breath held too long, and then caught again. The mangoes shifted. The smallest of the children gripped the edge of the bench until her knuckles paled. Out here, beyond the shelter of the mangroves, the wind found us, and the boat began to lift and drop, lift and drop, each slap of the hull louder than the last. The lagoon kept its own counsel; it gave nothing away about what lay beneath.

Mr Okafor did not look worried. He had been crossing this water for thirty-one years, he told me later, twice a day, in every season. He stood at the stern with one hand resting lightly on the tiller, as if the boat were an old dog that only needed reminding. When the engine coughed again, he laughed, a short, warm sound, and patted the motor's casing. 'She complains,' he said, 'but she has never yet refused.'

By the time the island school rose out of the mist, painted blue and absurdly cheerful, the sun had broken through. I stepped onto the jetty with legs that did not quite belong to me, and I realised I was no longer afraid of the water. I was afraid of the classroom.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give two phrases from paragraph 1 that show the narrator was nervous.

markingPoints.text: 'awake since four'
'packed and repacked twice'
'my hands would not keep it still'
'left half of it cooling on the step' (too anxious to drink)

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates found one phrase. Some copied the whole paragraph, which cannot be credited: select the precise words.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: At what time did the boat leave the jetty?

markingPoints.text: 5:40 (accept twenty to six)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by 'The lagoon kept its own counsel'.

markingPoints.text: the lagoon gave no clues / revealed nothing
about what was under the surface / what might happen, so the passengers could not predict any danger

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who repeated words from the phrase, such as 'counsel', could not show understanding. Own words are essential.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: For how many years had Mr Okafor been crossing the lagoon?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Identify and explain the effect of the image 'the water was a sheet of hammered pewter' in paragraph 2.

markingPoints.text: identifies it as a metaphor
suggests the water is flat, still and grey / dull in the early light
creates a cold, heavy or unwelcoming mood that matches the narrator's anxiety

parts.examinerComment: Naming the technique earns little on its own. The best answers explained what the image makes the reader see and feel.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how the writer uses language to create tension in paragraph 3.

markingPoints.text: the simile 'like a breath held too long' makes the reader wait anxiously with the passengers
'knuckles paled' shows fear through physical detail
repetition of 'lift and drop' recreates the relentless motion of the boat
'louder than the last' suggests the danger is growing
personification: the wind 'found us', as if hunting them

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers selected precise words and explained their effect. Weaker answers retold what happens in the paragraph.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: How does the writer present Mr Okafor in paragraph 4? Refer to the language used.

markingPoints.text: calm and experienced: 'thirty-one years … in every season'
relaxed control: 'one hand resting lightly on the tiller'
affectionate towards his boat: the 'old dog' simile / 'patted the motor's casing'
warm and humorous: 'she complains … but she has never yet refused'

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who contrasted Mr Okafor's calm with the passengers' fear showed good understanding of the writer's purpose.

questions.stem:
Passage B: Before You Set Out

Every summer, visitors arrive at Carrow Bay expecting a gentle seaside. The bay is beautiful, but it is not gentle. Local lifeboat crews were called out forty-three times last year, and most of the people they rescued had underestimated the water.

The first danger is the tide. At Carrow the sea goes out almost two kilometres, revealing wide sandbanks that invite walkers to explore. When the tide turns, it comes back faster than a person can walk, filling the channels behind them first, so that they find themselves stranded on shrinking islands of sand.

Then there are rip currents: narrow, fast-moving channels of water flowing away from the shore. They are hard to see from the beach, where they can look like calm, darker patches between the breaking waves. A swimmer caught in one is carried out to sea, and those who try to swim straight back against it quickly become exhausted.

Fog is another hazard. It can roll in from the sea within minutes, hiding landmarks and leaving people unable to tell which direction leads back to land. Even on a hot day, the water itself is cold enough to cause cold-water shock, a gasp reflex that can make a person breathe in water before they have had time to think.

None of this means visitors should stay away. Check the tide times before you walk out onto the sands, and set off back well before the tide turns. Swim only between the red and yellow flags, where lifeguards are watching. If you are caught in a rip current, do not fight it: swim parallel to the shore until you are free of it. And if you see someone in trouble, call the coastguard rather than going in after them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: How many times were lifeboat crews called out last year?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: According to Passage B, what makes the sea at Carrow Bay dangerous? Write your answer in note form. You do not need to use your own words.

markingPoints.text: the tide comes in faster than a person can walk
channels fill behind walkers, stranding them on sandbanks
rip currents are hard to see / look calm
rip currents carry swimmers out to sea and exhaust those who swim against them
fog arrives within minutes and hides landmarks / people lose their direction
the water is cold enough to cause cold-water shock, even on hot days
visitors underestimate the water

parts.examinerComment: Each note should contain one distinct point. Some candidates included the safety advice, which did not answer the question.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Give two pieces of advice the writer gives for staying safe at Carrow Bay.

markingPoints.text: check tide times / return well before the tide turns
swim only between the red and yellow flags
swim parallel to the shore if caught in a rip current
call the coastguard instead of going in after someone

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Using your notes from (b), write a summary of the dangers at Carrow Bay. Write no more than 120 words, using your own words as far as possible.

markingPoints.text: includes at least four relevant dangers
includes six or more relevant dangers, accurately
uses own words throughout, not copied phrases
concise, clearly organised and no more than 120 words

parts.examinerComment: The best summaries grouped related points, such as both effects of the tide, in a single sentence. Lifting whole sentences from the passage limits the writing marks.

questions.stem:
A message from the Head Teacher

From next term, mobile phones will not be allowed anywhere in school during the school day. Phones will be handed in at the gate each morning and returned at 3.30 pm. Teachers tell me that phones distract students in lessons, and some parents worry about online bullying during break times. Students who need to contact home will be able to use the telephone in the school office. I believe this change will help everyone to focus on learning and on each other.

parts.prompt: Write a letter to the Head Teacher giving your views on the plan to ban mobile phones during the school day. In your letter you should evaluate the reasons given and explain what you think the school should do. Base your letter on what you have read, but use your own words. Write 250 to 350 words.

markingPoints.text: Reading: uses and develops at least four relevant ideas from the text
Reading: evaluates the ideas and gives your own judgement, rather than just repeating them
Writing: register and format suit the audience and purpose
Writing: well structured, with a clear sequence and linked paragraphs
Writing: precise, varied vocabulary and sentence structures
Writing: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

parts.examinerComment: The best letters weighed each reason in the message instead of simply agreeing or disagreeing. Weaker responses listed the ideas without judging them.

parts.prompt: Describe a market at the moment it opens in the morning. Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: creates a clear, consistent atmosphere
Content: uses precise, original detail that appeals to several senses, avoiding clichés
Structure: organised deliberately, with controlled shifts of focus, viewpoint or time; avoids drifting into a story
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: The most effective descriptions focused on small, precise details and changes in light and sound as the market woke up. Some candidates drifted into a narrative about buying something.

questions.stem:
Notice to residents

The council is considering turning the unused car park on Mill Street into a community garden. The garden would include vegetable plots for local families, a play area and seating for older residents. Supporters say it would bring neighbours together and give children somewhere safe to play. Some local shopkeepers are concerned that losing the car park will mean fewer customers. A residents' meeting will be held next month before a decision is made.

parts.prompt: You have been asked to give a speech at the residents' meeting about the plan for a community garden. In your speech you should evaluate the arguments for and against, and say what you think the council should decide. Base your speech on what you have read, but use your own words. Write 250 to 350 words.

markingPoints.text: Reading: uses and develops at least four relevant ideas from the text
Reading: evaluates the ideas and gives your own judgement, rather than just repeating them
Writing: register and format suit the audience and purpose
Writing: well structured, with a clear sequence and linked paragraphs
Writing: precise, varied vocabulary and sentence structures
Writing: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

parts.examinerComment: Successful speeches addressed the audience directly and used rhetorical techniques sparingly. Some candidates forgot the shopkeepers' concerns, which limited the evaluation.

parts.prompt: Write a story that begins: 'The message was only four words long.' Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: a convincing plot with a clear purpose and a satisfying ending
Content: believable characters and setting, developed through detail
Structure: carefully paced, with an effective opening and controlled tension
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: Good stories made the four-word message central to the plot. Endings that were rushed or relied on 'it was all a dream' weakened otherwise strong work.

questions.stem:
Is homework worth it?

Some teachers argue that homework helps students practise new skills, builds independence and prepares them for exams. Others point out that students already spend six hours a day in lessons, and that long homework tasks leave little time for sport, family or rest. Research suggests that short, focused tasks are more useful than long ones, and that the value of homework depends on whether teachers give feedback on it.

parts.prompt: Write an article for your school magazine with the title 'Is homework worth it?'. In your article you should evaluate the views in the text and give your own opinion on how homework should be set. Base your article on what you have read, but use your own words. Write 250 to 350 words.

markingPoints.text: Reading: uses and develops at least four relevant ideas from the text
Reading: evaluates the ideas and gives your own judgement, rather than just repeating them
Writing: register and format suit the audience and purpose
Writing: well structured, with a clear sequence and linked paragraphs
Writing: precise, varied vocabulary and sentence structures
Writing: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

parts.examinerComment: Articles that proposed a balanced, practical policy were the most convincing. A clear headline and engaging opening helped establish the magazine register.

parts.prompt: Describe a place that has been abandoned. Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: creates a clear, consistent atmosphere
Content: uses precise, original detail that appeals to several senses, avoiding clichés
Structure: organised deliberately, with controlled shifts of focus, viewpoint or time; avoids drifting into a story
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: Strong responses suggested the place's past through carefully chosen objects. Lists of adjectives without a controlling mood were less successful.

questions.stem:
My year volunteering

Last year I spent twelve months volunteering at a wildlife rescue centre before university. The work was exhausting: early starts, cleaning enclosures and very little pay. But I learned more about responsibility than in any classroom, and I made friends from six different countries. Some of my friends think I wasted a year that I could have spent earning money or studying. I don't regret a single day.

parts.prompt: Your friend is deciding whether to spend a year volunteering before continuing their studies. Write a letter to your friend, evaluating the writer's experience and advising them what to do. Base your letter on what you have read, but use your own words. Write 250 to 350 words.

markingPoints.text: Reading: uses and develops at least four relevant ideas from the text
Reading: evaluates the ideas and gives your own judgement, rather than just repeating them
Writing: register and format suit the audience and purpose
Writing: well structured, with a clear sequence and linked paragraphs
Writing: precise, varied vocabulary and sentence structures
Writing: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

parts.examinerComment: An informal but controlled register suited this task well. The strongest letters considered whether the writer's experience would apply to their friend.

parts.prompt: Write a story with the title 'The Return'. Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: a convincing plot with a clear purpose and a satisfying ending
Content: believable characters and setting, developed through detail
Structure: carefully paced, with an effective opening and controlled tension
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: The title was interpreted in many interesting ways. The best stories used a limited time frame and developed one or two characters convincingly.

questions.stem:
Passage C: The Ovens

The bakery on Saltmarket Lane opened at six, but my grandfather's day began at half past two. That summer I was fourteen and had begged to help him, imagining warm bread and quiet conversation. Instead there was a bare bulb, a floor gritty with flour and a silence so complete that I could hear the clock above the sink deciding each second.

Grandad did not talk while he worked. His hands did the talking. They folded and turned the dough with a rhythm that never hurried and never paused, the way a tide comes in. When I tried to copy him, my dough tore and stuck to my fingers like wet cloth. He watched for a while, then reached across without a word and laid his floury hand over mine, pressing once, twice, until I felt what he meant.

At four the ovens were ready. He swung the iron doors open and the heat leapt out at us, a dry, roaring animal that had been waiting all night. My eyebrows prickled. Grandad slid the first trays in with a long wooden paddle, as calmly as if he were posting letters.

Then came the smell. It crept out of the ovens slowly at first and then filled every corner of the room, sweet and dark and faintly burnt at the edges, until the whole bakery seemed to be breathing it. Outside, the street was still black. A single delivery van grumbled past. Somewhere a dog barked once and thought better of it.

By six the shelves were full and the first customers were stamping their feet on the step. Grandad wiped his hands on his apron, nodded at the loaves I had shaped, crooked and lumpy among his perfect ones, and said the only full sentence I heard from him all morning: 'Those will sell first. People like bread that looks as if somebody made it.'

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: At what time did the narrator's grandfather begin work each day?

markingPoints.text: half past two / 2.30 (am)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered. A few candidates gave six o'clock, which is when the bakery opened, not when work began.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain, using your own words, how the narrator's expectations of working in the bakery differed from what the narrator found, in paragraph 1.

markingPoints.text: the narrator expected it to be cosy / pleasant (warm bread)
the narrator expected to chat / spend time talking with the grandfather
in fact it was bleak / basic / dusty (bare bulb, floury floor)
in fact it was totally silent / there was no conversation

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers made both sides of the contrast clear. Copying 'warm bread and quiet conversation' without explanation showed only partial understanding.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: What does the grandfather's final comment suggest about what he thinks of the narrator's loaves? Explain your answer.

markingPoints.text: he values them / is quietly proud of the narrator / approves of the narrator's work
he suggests their imperfection shows they are hand-made, which customers prefer / he is kindly turning a weakness into a strength

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates saw that the comment was kind. Fewer explained why the 'crooked and lumpy' shape becomes a selling point.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Identify and explain the effect of the image 'the heat leapt out at us, a dry, roaring animal that had been waiting all night' in paragraph 3.

markingPoints.text: identifies the metaphor / personification of the heat as an animal
'leapt' suggests the heat is sudden and forceful, almost attacking them
'roaring' conveys the noise and fierce intensity of the ovens
'waiting all night' makes the ovens seem alive, patient and slightly menacing / creates a sense of danger for the young narrator

parts.examinerComment: Effective answers explored individual words such as 'leapt' and 'roaring' rather than simply saying the image was 'vivid'.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain how the writer uses language to present the grandfather as skilled and calm in paragraphs 2 and 3.

markingPoints.text: 'His hands did the talking' suggests skill is expressed through action not words / he is expert and wordless
tide simile: his rhythm is natural, steady and unstoppable
'never hurried and never paused': balanced repetition shows unbroken control
contrast with the narrator's dough 'like wet cloth' highlights his expertise
'as calmly as if he were posting letters' shows that a dangerous task is routine to him

parts.examinerComment: The best responses selected short quotations and explained what each word suggests. Some candidates only listed techniques.

parts.label: (f)
parts.prompt: Explain how the writer uses the senses to create the atmosphere of the early morning in paragraph 4.

markingPoints.text: smell 'crept' / 'filled every corner': personification shows it spreading gradually until it dominates
'sweet and dark and faintly burnt': layered adjectives (polysyndeton) make the smell rich and precise
'the whole bakery seemed to be breathing it': the room is alive / warmth inside contrasts with the dark street
sounds of the van 'grumbled' and the single bark emphasise the stillness / quiet of the town

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers noticed the contrast between the warm, full bakery and the empty street outside. The humour of the dog that 'thought better of it' was well explained by some.

questions.stem:
Passage D: Screaming Parties

Every May, the skies above our town fill with dark, sickle-shaped birds that race between the rooftops in noisy groups. Locals call these gatherings 'screaming parties'. The birds are swifts, and they have just completed a journey of several thousand kilometres from Africa. Yet each year fewer of them arrive.

Swifts are astonishingly well suited to life in the air. They feed, drink and even sleep on the wing, and a young swift may not land at all for its first two or three years. The one thing they cannot do in the sky is raise their young. For that they need a dark, dry gap high up on a building: a hole under the roof tiles, a crack beneath the gutter. Swifts are loyal to these sites and return to the same hole year after year.

That loyalty has become a problem. When old houses are repaired, the gaps under their roofs are often sealed to keep heat in. New buildings are designed with smooth, tight surfaces that offer nowhere to nest. A pair of swifts returning from Africa may simply find their doorway bricked up, and with no time to search, they fail to breed that summer.

Food is a second difficulty. Swifts eat only flying insects, catching thousands a day to feed their chicks. Where gardens are paved over and pesticides are used heavily, there are fewer insects in the air, and the parents must fly further to find enough.

The good news is that helping swifts is cheap and simple. Special swift bricks, with a hollow nesting space inside, can be built into new walls at almost no extra cost. Nest boxes can be fixed under the eaves of existing houses. Builders can be asked to leave old nest holes open when they repair a roof. Gardeners can plant flowers that attract insects and avoid sprays. In our town, a survey last summer recorded 26 nesting pairs; the volunteers who counted them hope that, with a little help, the screaming parties will grow louder again.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: How many nesting pairs of swifts did the survey in the writer's town record last summer?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: According to Passage D, why are fewer swifts returning each year? Write your answer in note form. You do not need to use your own words.

markingPoints.text: swifts need dark, dry gaps high on buildings to nest
gaps are sealed when old houses are repaired / to keep heat in
new buildings have smooth, tight surfaces with nowhere to nest
swifts return to the same site, so if it is blocked they fail to breed (no time to search)
fewer flying insects because gardens are paved over
pesticides reduce insects, so parents must fly further for food

parts.examinerComment: Each note should contain a single, distinct point. Some candidates included the solutions from paragraph 5, which do not answer this question.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Write a summary of the ways people can help swifts, as described in Passage D. Write no more than 100 words, using your own words as far as possible.

markingPoints.text: includes at least three relevant ways of helping
includes five relevant ways: swift bricks in new walls; nest boxes under eaves; keep old nest holes open during roof repairs; plant insect-attracting flowers; avoid pesticide sprays
uses own words throughout, not copied phrases
concise, clearly organised and within the word limit

parts.examinerComment: Good summaries grouped the building measures and the garden measures together. Including the reasons for decline wasted words and was not credited.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain, using your own words, why swifts are described in paragraph 2 as 'astonishingly well suited to life in the air'. Give two details from the paragraph.

markingPoints.text: they eat / drink in flight
they can sleep while flying
young birds can stay airborne for two or three years without landing

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates found two details. Answers that simply repeated 'well suited to life in the air' could not be credited.

questions.stem:
Passage E: The Year the River Came

That year the rain did not fall so much as lean on us. For eleven days it pressed against the windows, drummed on the tin roof of the shed and turned the lane outside our house into a brown, muttering stream.

My father spent those days pretending to be calm. He moved the photograph albums upstairs 'just in case', then the rugs, then, with a little laugh that did not reach his eyes, the television. My mother filled every pan we owned with clean water and lined them up on the landing like soldiers.

On the twelfth night the river arrived. It did not crash through the door as I had imagined. It slid under it, quiet as a thief, and spread across the kitchen floor in a thin, glittering sheet that grew a centimetre at a time. By morning the chairs were standing up to their knees in it. Our shoes floated past the bottom stair like small, abandoned boats.

When the water finally sank away, it left behind a tidemark on the walls at exactly the height of my shoulder, and a smell that I can still summon if I close my eyes: mud, rot and something sweetish, like fruit left too long in a bowl. Everything we had not carried upstairs was ruined. The sofa was a sodden carcass. My mother's piano, which nobody played but everybody loved, gave a single drowned note when she touched it and never made a sound again.

What I remember most, though, is not the damage. It is the morning after, when neighbours we had barely spoken to arrived with buckets, brooms and flasks of tea, and stayed until dark.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by the phrase 'with a little laugh that did not reach his eyes' in paragraph 2.

markingPoints.text: the father's laugh was forced / not genuine
he was hiding his anxiety / fear about the flood from his family

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates understood that the father was worried. Stronger answers linked this to 'pretending to be calm'.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how the writer uses language to convey the arrival of the flood water in paragraph 3.

markingPoints.text: contrast with expectation: it did 'not crash' but 'slid', making it quieter and more unsettling
simile 'quiet as a thief' suggests something sly, unwelcome, stealing the family's possessions
'thin, glittering sheet' is deceptively beautiful / harmless-looking
'a centimetre at a time' conveys a slow, relentless rise
chairs 'up to their knees' / shoes 'like small, abandoned boats': personification and simile show how familiar objects are overwhelmed and lost

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers explored how the writer makes the flood frightening because it is quiet. Weaker answers retold events.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Re-read paragraphs 1 and 4. Select four powerful words or phrases from these paragraphs, including imagery, and explain how the writer uses them to convey the power and effects of the flood.

markingPoints.text: selects at least four precise, relevant words or phrases, including imagery, drawn from both paragraphs
explains the meaning of each choice accurately in context
explores connotations and effects precisely, showing how images work (not just naming techniques)
shows how the choices combine to create an overall impression of the flood's power and its aftermath

parts.examinerComment: Useful choices included 'lean on us' (the rain as a heavy, oppressive weight); 'drummed' (relentless noise); 'brown, muttering stream' (the lane transformed, threatening voice); 'tidemark … at exactly the height of my shoulder' (the scale measured against the child's body); 'sodden carcass' (sofa as a dead animal, decay); 'single drowned note' (the piano 'dies', loss of something loved). The best answers treated each image separately and explored its connotations in detail. Answers that named techniques without explaining the effect stayed in the middle levels. Selecting overlong quotations made precise comment difficult.

questions.stem:
Passage F: Two Wheels, One City

Three years ago, the city of Harlow Vale introduced a bicycle-sharing scheme. Anyone with a mobile phone can unlock one of 800 bicycles from a docking station, ride it across the city and leave it at any other station. The council says the scheme has changed the way people travel, and most of the evidence supports that claim.

The most obvious benefit is cost. A ride of up to thirty minutes is free for members, and an annual membership costs less than a month of bus tickets. Students and shift workers, who often travel when buses are infrequent, have been among the keenest users.

Journeys are also quicker than many people expect. In the crowded centre, where traffic crawls during the rush hour, a bicycle is often the fastest way to cross town, and riders never have to search for a parking space.

There are benefits for health, too. Regular cycling builds fitness without the need for a gym, and a local doctors' group reports that patients who began cycling to work say they feel less stressed. Fewer car journeys have also meant cleaner air on the main roads, which matters to the many residents with asthma.

The scheme is not perfect. Docking stations in the city centre are sometimes empty at peak times, while those on the outskirts are full, and riders complain that some cycle lanes stop suddenly at busy junctions. The council has promised more stations and safer, joined-up routes by next year.

questions.stem:
Passage G: Mend It, Don't End It

When the zip on a coat breaks or a lamp stops working, most of us do not even consider repairing it. Things are cheap, repair shops have vanished from the high street, and we have been taught to shrug and buy another. A growing movement of Repair Cafés is trying to change that habit.

The idea is simple. On the first Saturday of every month, our local community hall fills with long tables, toolboxes and sewing machines. Anyone can bring in something broken, put their name on a list and wait with a cup of tea until a volunteer is free. There is no charge, although a jar by the door accepts donations towards spare parts.

The volunteers are the heart of the café. There is a retired electrician, a seamstress who once made costumes for the theatre and a bicycle mechanic who arrives with grease still on his hands. They work with the patience of surgeons, and they have coaxed radios, kettles and children's toys back to life. They refuse to take a penny; their only payment, one told me, is the grin on someone's face when a dead machine hums again.

The benefits go well beyond fixing things. Every item mended is one less thing thrown into landfill, and visitors save money they would have spent on replacements. Crucially, owners are encouraged to sit beside the volunteer and watch, so they leave knowing how to do the repair themselves next time. In this way, skills that older people learnt decades ago are being handed on to teenagers who have never held a soldering iron.

The café is also a place to meet. Neighbours who have lived on the same street for years without speaking now chat while they wait, and several regular visitors say it is the only time in the month they talk to anyone outside their family. For the volunteers, many of them retired, it offers a sense of being useful again.

Last month, a woman brought in a toaster that had belonged to her mother. It took two volunteers an hour to find the fault, but when the first slice popped up, the whole hall applauded. 'Some things you just can't replace,' she said.

questions.stem:
Passage A: The Crossing

I had been awake since four, listening to the generator next door cough itself into life. My school bag sat by the door, packed and repacked twice. When my mother handed me a cup of tea, my hands would not keep it still, and I left half of it cooling on the step.

The boat left the jetty at 5:40, exactly as Mr Okafor had promised. There were six of us on board: four children in pressed white shirts, a woman with a basket of mangoes, and me. Nobody spoke. At that hour the water was a sheet of hammered pewter, and the far shore was nothing more than a rumour of trees.

Halfway across, the engine faltered. It did not stop; it hesitated, like a breath held too long, and then caught again. The mangoes shifted. The smallest of the children gripped the edge of the bench until her knuckles paled. Out here, beyond the shelter of the mangroves, the wind found us, and the boat began to lift and drop, lift and drop, each slap of the hull louder than the last. The lagoon kept its own counsel; it gave nothing away about what lay beneath.

Mr Okafor did not look worried. He had been crossing this water for thirty-one years, he told me later, twice a day, in every season. He stood at the stern with one hand resting lightly on the tiller, as if the boat were an old dog that only needed reminding. When the engine coughed again, he laughed, a short, warm sound, and patted the motor's casing. 'She complains,' he said, 'but she has never yet refused.'

By the time the island school rose out of the mist, painted blue and absurdly cheerful, the sun had broken through. I stepped onto the jetty with legs that did not quite belong to me, and I realised I was no longer afraid of the water. I was afraid of the classroom.

parts.label: (a)

parts.examinerComment: Useful choices included 'a sheet of hammered pewter' (cold, hard, grey and still, an uninviting surface); 'a rumour of trees' (the shore barely visible, uncertain); 'hesitated, like a breath held too long' (the engine personified, mirroring the passengers' suspense); 'until her knuckles paled' (physical fear shown through a small detail); 'lift and drop, lift and drop' (repetition imitating the boat's motion); 'kept its own counsel' (the lagoon as secretive, hiding danger). The best answers explored each image separately.

questions.stem:
Passage C: The Ovens

The bakery on Saltmarket Lane opened at six, but my grandfather's day began at half past two. That summer I was fourteen and had begged to help him, imagining warm bread and quiet conversation. Instead there was a bare bulb, a floor gritty with flour and a silence so complete that I could hear the clock above the sink deciding each second.

Grandad did not talk while he worked. His hands did the talking. They folded and turned the dough with a rhythm that never hurried and never paused, the way a tide comes in. When I tried to copy him, my dough tore and stuck to my fingers like wet cloth. He watched for a while, then reached across without a word and laid his floury hand over mine, pressing once, twice, until I felt what he meant.

At four the ovens were ready. He swung the iron doors open and the heat leapt out at us, a dry, roaring animal that had been waiting all night. My eyebrows prickled. Grandad slid the first trays in with a long wooden paddle, as calmly as if he were posting letters.

Then came the smell. It crept out of the ovens slowly at first and then filled every corner of the room, sweet and dark and faintly burnt at the edges, until the whole bakery seemed to be breathing it. Outside, the street was still black. A single delivery van grumbled past. Somewhere a dog barked once and thought better of it.

By six the shelves were full and the first customers were stamping their feet on the step. Grandad wiped his hands on his apron, nodded at the loaves I had shaped, crooked and lumpy among his perfect ones, and said the only full sentence I heard from him all morning: 'Those will sell first. People like bread that looks as if somebody made it.'

questions.stem:
Passage E: The Year the River Came

That year the rain did not fall so much as lean on us. For eleven days it pressed against the windows, drummed on the tin roof of the shed and turned the lane outside our house into a brown, muttering stream.

My father spent those days pretending to be calm. He moved the photograph albums upstairs 'just in case', then the rugs, then, with a little laugh that did not reach his eyes, the television. My mother filled every pan we owned with clean water and lined them up on the landing like soldiers.

On the twelfth night the river arrived. It did not crash through the door as I had imagined. It slid under it, quiet as a thief, and spread across the kitchen floor in a thin, glittering sheet that grew a centimetre at a time. By morning the chairs were standing up to their knees in it. Our shoes floated past the bottom stair like small, abandoned boats.

When the water finally sank away, it left behind a tidemark on the walls at exactly the height of my shoulder, and a smell that I can still summon if I close my eyes: mud, rot and something sweetish, like fruit left too long in a bowl. Everything we had not carried upstairs was ruined. The sofa was a sodden carcass. My mother's piano, which nobody played but everybody loved, gave a single drowned note when she touched it and never made a sound again.

What I remember most, though, is not the damage. It is the morning after, when neighbours we had barely spoken to arrived with buckets, brooms and flasks of tea, and stayed until dark.

parts.prompt:

parts.examinerComment: Effective interviews gave the mother a convincing voice and developed implied details, such as the father's forced calm and the loss of the piano. Answers that only listed the damage missed the third bullet, which carries the passage's emotional turn.

Writing: precise, varied vocabulary and sentence structures
Writing: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

parts.examinerComment: Stronger letters proposed workable compromises, such as exemptions for blue-badge holders or early delivery windows, which showed genuine evaluation. Weaker letters simply listed points for and against. A formal register suited the audience; some letters were too casual for a councillor.

parts.prompt: Describe a busy open-air market in the moments just before it closes for the day. Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: creates a clear, consistent atmosphere
Content: uses precise, original detail that appeals to several senses, avoiding clichés
Structure: organised deliberately, with controlled shifts of focus, viewpoint or time; avoids drifting into a story
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: Strong responses used the closing of the market to give the writing a clear shape, contrasting the last burst of noise with the emptying stalls. Lists of goods for sale, without atmosphere, limited the marks.

parts.prompt: Write a story in which a character returns to a place they have not visited since childhood. Write 350 to 450 words.

markingPoints.text: Content: a convincing plot with a clear purpose and a satisfying ending
Content: believable characters and setting, developed through detail
Structure: carefully paced, with an effective opening and controlled tension
Style: wide, precise vocabulary chosen for effect
Style: varied sentence structures used for effect
Accuracy: spelling, punctuation and grammar are accurate throughout

parts.examinerComment: The best stories used the contrast between memory and the present to reveal something about the character. Some candidates spent too long on the journey and left little room for the return itself.
